title: A Radio Interview on Rewilding an Abandoned Farm
script: Host: [warmly] This morning I'm joined by Rani, who turned her late father's abandoned farm into a rewilding project. Welcome.
Host: [curious] For listeners unfamiliar with the term, what exactly does rewilding mean in practice, on an actual piece of land?
Guest: [thoughtful] Essentially, it means stepping back and letting natural processes take over again, rather than continuing to control every inch the way farming requires.
Host: [interested] That sounds almost counterintuitive. Wouldn't neglecting the land simply lead to it becoming an overgrown mess?
Guest: [smiling] That's exactly what my neighbors said at first, and honestly, for the first year, it did look somewhat chaotic and unplanned.
Guest: [confidently] However, by the second year, native grasses returned on their own, and insects I hadn't seen since childhood started appearing throughout the fields.
Host: [surprised] Even though you weren't actively planting anything yourself during that whole process?
Guest: [explaining] Correct, though I did remove some invasive plants early on, since those would have prevented native species from establishing themselves properly.
Host: [curious] What was the hardest emotional part of watching your father's organized farm transform into something so different from what he built?

Guest: [honestly] Accepting that honoring his memory didn't necessarily mean preserving the farm exactly as he left it, despite what I initially assumed. In spite of that early guilt, I eventually realized he loved this land itself, not merely the crops growing on it.
Host: [thoughtful] Has wildlife actually returned in noticeable numbers, or is that mostly aspirational at this stage?
Guest: [warmly] Genuinely noticeable. We now have owls nesting in the old barn, deer passing through regularly, and a small stream that had dried up decades ago started flowing again.
Host: [curious] What would you tell someone considering a similar project on their own unused land?
Guest: [encouraging] Be patient, because nature moves on its own schedule, and results that seem invisible in year one often become undeniable by year three.
Host: [warmly] That's a beautiful way to close this. Thank you so much for sharing your father's land and its transformation with us today, Rani.
Guest: [warmly] Thank you for having me. I hope it encourages someone listening to try something similar with their own quiet corner of land.
